The abstract details match: 178 studies with n=5097 in the strength network, 119 with n=3364 in the hypertrophy network, higher-load (>80% 1RM) prescriptions maximised strength, and hypertrophy was comparable across prescriptions. A search for retraction or correction found no notice. | I did NOT verify the top-ranked prescription SMD of 1.60 (1.38-1.82) or the 'highly robust' threshold analysis. My last search for them was refused because the shared web search budget was used up. I also did not confirm from the abstract that the network was restricted to randomised trials. Comparisons between loads are indirect, run through a common control. Unlike the proposed statement, the analysis is not conditioned on sets taken to failure. The researcher's population (healthy adults) and design are consistent with what I saw.

sources.title: Influence of resistance training load on measures of skeletal muscle hypertrophy and improvements in maximal strength and neuromuscular task performance: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Refalo MC, Hamilton DL, Paval DR, Gallagher IJ, Feros SA, Fyfe JJ
sources.design: Systematic review with meta-analysis of 45 studies (4,713 records identified). It compared higher-load (>60% 1RM or <15RM) with lower-load (<=60% 1RM or >=15RM) RT.
sources.population: Adults; higher load (>60% 1RM or <15RM) vs lower load (≤60% 1RM or ≥15RM)
sources.sampleSize: 45 studies (from 4,713 screened records); participant total not seen
sources.found: A meta-analysis of 45 studies. Higher loads gave larger 1RM gains (effect size 0.34, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.52) and isometric gains (0.41, 0.07 to 0.76). Muscle growth was similar (whole-muscle effect size 0.06, -0.11 to 0.24), and the 1RM advantage was smaller in older adults (0.20 vs 0.34).
sources.limitations: It defined higher load broadly (above 60% of 1RM or fewer than 15 reps), so it cannot confirm the 80% threshold specifically.

verification.notes: The PubMed record for PMID 33874848 matches: Refalo MC et al., J Sports Sci 2021 Aug;39(15):1723-1745, epub 19 Apr 2021, DOI 10.1080/02640414.2021.1898094. The Taylor & Francis page agrees (Vol 39, No 15). The abstract confirms 45 studies (from 4,713), similar hypertrophy (whole-body lean mass P=0.70), and a 1RM advantage for higher load (ES 0.34) that was larger in younger participants. No erratum, correction or retraction was found. The one correction notice in the results was for a different paper (on hypoxia training). | I confirmed the ES values and CIs. I did not see the P values (0.70, 0.47, 0.0003, 0.02) or an explicit statement that the 1RM effect was non-significant in older adults. I only saw that it was smaller (0.20 vs 0.34). I searched for the researcher's quote, but the results paraphrased it and never showed it word for word, so quoteVerbatim is false. Caveat: 'higher load' here means >60% 1RM or <15RM. That is much broader than the proposed statement's >=80% 1RM, so this source supports heavier > lighter in general, not specifically >=80%.

One search summary claimed it was in the abstract but did not reproduce it, so quoteVerbatim is false. I saw no participant total. The hypertrophy conclusion rests on whole-muscle measures, because a biopsy (fibre) meta-analysis could not be performed. sources.title: The influence of resistance exercise training prescription variables on skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function in healthy adults: An umbrella review

sources.journal: Journal of Sport and Health Science

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Fiatarone Singh MA, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, Steen JP, Thomas GA, Triplett NT, Washington TA, Werner TJ, Phillips SM

sources.title: Non-Specific Strength Changes Between High- and Low-Load Isotonic Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Hammert WB, Kataoka, Yamada, Sallberg, Kang, Buckner, Loenneke JP
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PubMed, Scopus, Embase searched to 14 June 2025): 10 studies from 7,885 unique articles, 44 effect sizes, 245 participants (high load n=114, low load n=131). Full-text snippet: high load >60% 1RM, low load <=40% 1RM.

sources.sampleSize: 10 studies, 44 effect sizes, 245 participants (high load n=114, low load n=131)
sources.found: A meta-analysis of 10 studies with 245 participants. On strength tests not used in training (isometric or isokinetic), the advantage of heavy loads was inconclusive: d=0.32, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.72, p=0.10.

The Springer and PMC pages have the same title. The Springer abstract confirms that PubMed, Scopus and Embase were searched to 14 June 2025, that 10 studies were included, and the result d=0.322 (SE 0.17), 95% CI -0.08 to 0.72, p=0.104, which was inconclusive. It went online in 2025, so the year depends on whether you use the online or issue date. I did not see the volume and pages (56:763-773) myself, or the other authors' initials. No correction or retraction was found. | The result is null/inconclusive. It does not support a heavy-load advantage beyond the trained lift. It does support the proposed statement's explicit caveat that transfer to non-specific strength tests is inconclusive, hence pass for that clause with direction mixed. The researcher's numbers match what I saw. I saw the researcher's quote only as a fragment ('the results of the current analysis were inconclusive'), not the full sentence, so quoteVerbatim is false. sources.title: Neither load nor systemic hormones determine resistance training-mediated hypertrophy or strength gains in resistance-trained young men
sources.authors: Morton et al.

It should be shown as counter-evidence, and the population note should say that in trained men one RCT found mostly no load effect on strength. sources.title: Effects of Low- vs. High-Load Resistance Training on Muscle Strength and Hypertrophy in Well-Trained Men

So the statement's 'only after total sleep deprivation' wording for strength is unconfirmed; the pooled strength effect across protocols was reported as significant. The researcher gave no quote. The verified quote is a fragment from a search snippet consistent with the abstract. I did not see the full PubMed page, so I could not check for retraction or erratum notices; none appeared in the results.

sources.title: Effects of sleep deprivation on sports performance and perceived exertion in athletes and non-athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Kong Y, Yu B, Guan G, Wang Y, He H
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled and randomized crossover trials (PROSPERO CRD42023492792, Cochrane RoB 2, searched to September 2024), 45 studies. Front Physiol 2025;16:1544286, PMID 40236824, PMC11996801.
sources.population: Athletes and healthy non-athletes exposed to total, early or late sleep deprivation
sources.sampleSize: 45 trials (16 aerobic endurance, 8 anaerobic endurance, 23 explosive power, 10 maximal force, 4 speed, 4 skill control, 12 RPE); participant total not seen
sources.found: Across 45 randomised and crossover trials, sleep deprivation lowered aerobic endurance, explosive power and maximal force in athletes (standardised effect sizes -0.66, -0.63 and -0.35). In non-athletes it lowered aerobic endurance (-1.02) but had no effect on explosive power (-0.02).
sources.limitations: It reports standardised effect sizes rather than percentages, and its results for perceived effort and for each type of sleep loss (early, late or total) were not verified.

verification.notes: The PubMed record for PMID 40236824 shows the title, Kong Y (Yan Kong, Beijing Sport University) as first author, Front Physiol 2025, and DOI 10.3389/fphys.2025.1544286. The PMC and Frontiers pages agree, give a publication date of 1 Apr 2025 and PROSPERO CRD42023492792, and list 45 studies. A search for retraction, expression of concern, erratum or corrigendum found no notice. | Design and the athlete AE/EP/MF effects match the researcher's summary. I did NOT see the RPE effect (SMD 0.47), the speed and skill-control results, the null anaerobic-endurance results, or the subgroup results by deprivation type (early, late, total). Those parts of the researcher's finding are unverified. Effects are SMDs, not percentages, so this paper backs the direction but not the '7-8%' size. Inconsistency to flag: the researcher's own summary says early-night deprivation mainly reduced explosive power and maximal force. That conflicts with the proposed statement's lines that strength is affected 'only after total sleep deprivation' and that a night of early-night restriction 'may have no meaningful effect'. If that subgroup result holds, the statement's strength and early-restriction wording needs revisiting. The null EP effect in non-athletes also shows the effect is not uniform. I saw only fragments of the abstract text, not whole sentences, so I set verifiedQuote to null. No retraction or erratum notices seen.

sources.title: Effects of Acute Sleep Deprivation on Sporting Performance in Athletes: A Comprehensive Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Gong M, Sun M, Sun Y, Jin L, Li S
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 studies (75 indicators per researcher; I saw the 27-study count) in athletes after acute sleep deprivation. Nat Sci Sleep 2024;16:935-948, DOI 10.2147/NSS.S467531.
sources.population: Athletes exposed to acute sleep deprivation (whole-night, or partial at the beginning or end of the night)
sources.sampleSize: 27 studies, 75 indicators; participant total not seen
sources.found: Across 27 studies in athletes, acute sleep deprivation lowered overall performance by a medium amount (effect size -0.56). The biggest effects were on high-intensity intermittent exercise (-1.57) and skill (-1.06) and the smallest on explosive power (-0.39); afternoon performance was hit harder than morning performance (-1.11 vs -0.30), and losing sleep at the end of the night was worst.
sources.limitations: It covers athletes only, and its results for each type of sleep loss, including a reportedly small effect of a full night without sleep, were not verified.

verification.notes: Searching the DOI 10.2147/NSS.S467531 returned the Dovepress (Nature and Science of Sleep vol 16) page and the DOAJ record. The title, authors (Gong M, Sun M, Sun Y, Jin L, Li S), Nat Sci Sleep 2024 Jul 9;16:935-948, 27 studies / 75 indicators and the overall effect of -0.56 all match. The proposer gave no PMID. A PubMed listing shows 'Gong M, et al. Nat Sci Sleep. 2024. PMID: 39006249 Free PMC article. Review.', so the paper is PubMed-indexed. The PMCID PMC11246080 came up as the full-text record in the search results. A search for retraction, expression of concern or erratum found no notice. | The abstract numbers I saw match the researcher's on overall effect, ability categories and time of day, and on late-night partial deprivation being worst. I did NOT see the per-protocol figures (-1.17 late, -0.23 whole-night, -0.25 early ns). If whole-night deprivation really is only -0.23, it is a weaker effect than the statement's 'skips sleep entirely' framing implies. I saw no PMID in results; the paper showed up in PubMed only as a 'cited by' entry with its bibliographic details. Population is athletes only. I saw the abstract only through search summaries, not verbatim sentences, so verifiedQuote is null. No retraction notice seen.

sources.title: Inadequate sleep and muscle strength: Implications for resistance training
sources.authors: Knowles OE, Drinkwater EJ, Urwin CS, Lamon S, Aisbett B
sources.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
sources.design: Systematic review (search of five electronic databases, no meta-analysis seen). J Sci Med Sport 2018;21(9):959-968, DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2018.01.012. I did not see the number of included studies (17 per the researcher).
sources.population: Adults in studies of sleep deprivation or restriction with resistance exercise or muscle strength outcomes
sources.found: This review of studies on sleep and resistance training found that several nights in a row of restricted sleep could reduce force in multi-joint lifts such as squats, but not in single-joint movements. Hormone responses to training were inconsistent.
sources.limitations: It is mainly about several nights of short sleep rather than one night, it did not pool results, and its PubMed record could not be confirmed (its DOI could).
sources.quote: Inadequate sleep impairs maximal muscle strength in compound movements when performed without specific interventions designed to increase motivation.

verification.notes: The DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2018.01.012 resolves to this paper on ScienceDirect and JSAMS. Those pages show authors Knowles OE, Drinkwater EJ, Urwin CS, Lamon S, Aisbett B, J Sci Med Sport, published online 3 Feb 2018, and ResearchGate gives vol 21(9). The 17 included studies and the main findings match the proposer's summary. PMID 29422383 could not be confirmed: two PubMed searches (by PMID and by exact title) did not return the record, and no page I saw showed that PMID. identifierResolves is therefore unknown even though the DOI is confirmed. A search for retraction, expression of concern, erratum or corrigendum found no notice. | The PubMed page for PMID 29422383 did not come up in search; the abstract text came from an author PDF copy, Semantic Scholar and ResearchGate. The researcher's sentence 'Sleep deprivation had little effect on muscle strength during resistance exercise' was not in the fragments I saw, so it is unverified. The positive strength finding comes from consecutive nights of restriction, a different, chronic exposure, not the acute single night in the claim. So the paper only partly supports the statement's acute-strength caveat, and 'mixed' is right. The conclusion that inadequate sleep impairs compound-lift strength is somewhat stronger than the statement's 'small and inconsistent'. No retraction notice seen.

sources.title: Implications of sleep loss or sleep deprivation on muscle strength: a systematic review
sources.authors: Easow J, et al.
sources.design: Systematic review without meta-analysis: 13 included studies with counterbalanced or randomised designs in healthy adults (514 database records plus 563 from organization and citation searching). Sleep Breath, published July 2025, PMID 40663194, PMC12263768, DOI 10.1007/s11325-025-03413-0.
sources.population: Adults exposed to acute or chronic sleep deprivation or restriction with muscle strength, power or muscular endurance outcomes
sources.sampleSize: 13 studies included (514 database records plus 563 from other sources screened); participant total not seen
sources.found: Across 13 studies in healthy adults, some found lower muscle strength after a night without sleep and others found no clear difference. Taken together, short- and longer-term sleep loss reduced some measures of strength, power and muscular endurance and increased fatigue.
sources.limitations: It is a review without pooled numbers that mixes one-night and longer-term sleep loss, so it cannot say how large the acute effect on strength is.
sources.quote: some studies reported a negative impact of sleep deprivation on strength performance, while others showed no significant differences following a night of sleep deprivation

verification.notes: The PubMed record for PMID 40663194 shows the title, Judy Easow as first author with nine co-authors (mostly Manipal Academy of Higher Education), Sleep and Breathing, published 15 Jul 2025, vol 29(4), article 242, and DOI 10.1007/s11325-025-03413-0. The PMC12263768 and repository pages give the same title. 13 studies were included and the findings were mixed. A search for retraction, expression of concern, erratum or correction found no notice. | The researcher's summary matches the abstract content I saw. Different search summaries worded the quote as 'after a night' and as 'following a night'; I used the version shown in quotation marks. Its support for the statement is limited to the strength caveat, where acute effects are inconsistent, and it pools acute with chronic exposure. I did not see the full author list. No retraction notice seen.

sources.title: Sleep and athletic performance: the effects of sleep loss on exercise performance, and physiological and cognitive responses to exercise
sources.authors: Fullagar HH, Skorski S, Duffield R, Hammes D, Coutts AJ, Meyer T
sources.design: Narrative review, context only. Sports Med 2015;45(2):161-186, PMID 25315456 (the researcher listed none), DOI 10.1007/s40279-014-0260-0.
sources.population: Athletes and exercising adults
sources.found: This earlier review describes how sleep restriction and deprivation affect exercise, the body and the mind. It reports slower and less accurate thinking after sleep loss, but concludes that the link between sleep loss and exercise performance was still unclear at the time.
sources.limitations: It is a narrative review that predates the meta-analyses and did not pool results, so it gives background only and cannot confirm the size or direction of the effect.
sources.quote: Based on this context, this review aims to evaluate the importance and prevalence of sleep in athletes and summarises the effects of sleep loss (restriction and deprivation) on exercise performance, and physiological and cognitive responses to exercise.

verification.notes: The Springer page for DOI 10.1007/s40279-014-0260-0 shows this title in Sports Medicine 45(2):161-186 (2015), first published online Oct 2014, with authors Fullagar HHK, Skorski S, Duffield R, Hammes D, Coutts AJ, Meyer T. A search result points to PubMed record PMID 25315456 with Sports Med. 2015 Feb;45(2):161-86. The proposer gave no PMID and no issue number, so I added both. It is a narrative review in a peer-reviewed, PubMed-indexed journal. The abstract says exercise performance is negatively affected after sleep loss, but that the extent and mechanisms remain uncertain or equivocal. A search for retraction, expression of concern or erratum found no notice. | The researcher's finding (impaired submaximal strength, endurance, reaction time, accuracy and vigor) came from a citing paper (PMID 31288293, a sleep-hygiene review), not from this paper's abstract. The abstract I saw instead describes the evidence on exercise performance as equivocal, so the stated finding is secondhand and does not match the abstract's emphasis. As a narrative review it is context only. I saw only part of the abstract. PubMed does index it as PMID 25315456.

sources.title: A Validation of Six Wearable Devices for Estimating Sleep, Heart Rate and Heart Rate Variability in Healthy Adults
sources.authors: Miller DJ, Sargent C, Roach GD
sources.design: Validation study against criterion references: polysomnography for sleep and ECG for heart rate/HRV. One laboratory night (9 h in bed, 23:00-08:00) with all six devices worn at once: Apple Watch S6, Garmin Forerunner 245 Music, Polar Vantage V, Oura Ring Gen 2, WHOOP 3.0, Somfit. n=53 (26 F, 27 M), age 25.4 +/- 5.9 y.
sources.population: Healthy adults (26 women, 27 men), mean age about 25 y. Devices: Apple Watch S6, Garmin Forerunner 245 Music, Polar Vantage V, Oura Ring Gen 2, WHOOP 3.0, Somfit.
sources.found: Across one laboratory night in 53 healthy young adults, six wearables agreed with polysomnography on sleep versus wake for about 86-89% of epochs, but for only about 50-65% on sleep stages. Against ECG, WHOOP read heart rate 0.3 bpm low (ICC 0.99) and HRV 4.5 ms low.
sources.limitations: It covers a single night in young healthy adults using older device models (Oura Gen 2, WHOOP 3.0), and heart rate and HRV figures were confirmed only for WHOOP.
sources.quote: Compared with ECG-derived heart rate (HR), WHOOP underestimated HR by an average of 0.3 beats per min, absolute bias was 0.7 beats per min, intraclass correlation was 0.99, and WHOOP underestimated HRV by an average of 4.5 ms.

verification.notes: The PubMed record for PMID 36016077 is this paper: Miller DJ, Sargent C, Roach GD, Sensors (Basel) 2022 Aug 22;22(16):6317, DOI 10.3390/s22166317, PMCID PMC9412437. PMC, the doi.org/MDPI page and DOAJ give the same title and citation. MDPI has a peer-review report page. A targeted search for retraction, erratum or correction found no notice, and the PubMed record showed none. | Confirmed: PMID 36016077, Sensors 2022;22(16):6317, DOI 10.3390/s22166317, authors Miller, Sargent, Roach. Confirmed numbers: sleep/wake 86-89%, staging about 50-65%, n=53, and the WHOOP HR/HRV figures. The WHOOP sentence was shown as MDPI article text and may come from the abstract or the body. NOT verified: Oura HR bias (+0.1 bpm, absolute bias 1.80 bpm, ICC 0.85), WHOOP HRV absolute bias 4.7 ms, and Polar's proportional HRV bias (+28.8 to -124.2 ms). Search snippets did not show them, so treat them as unconfirmed. A secondary blog summary says all six devices underestimated HRV. The sleep-staging and sleep/wake numbers in the proposed statement are directly supported. Only WHOOP's HR/HRV agreement is confirmed here. Single lab night in young healthy adults. Older device generations (Oura Gen 2, WHOOP 3.0).

sources.title: Validation of nocturnal resting heart rate and heart rate variability in consumer wearables
sources.authors: Dial MB, Hollander ME, Vatne EA, Emerson AM, Edwards NA, Hagen JA
sources.design: Validation study against an ECG reference worn at the same time as multiple consumer wearables during sleep (Lin's CCC, MAPE). Devices: Garmin Fenix 6, Oura Gen 3, Oura Gen 4, Polar Grit X Pro, WHOOP 4.0. n=13 healthy adults (6 female), 536 nights in total (repeated measures).
sources.population: Healthy adults (6 female). Devices: Garmin Fenix 6, Oura Gen 3, Oura Gen 4, Polar Grit X Pro, WHOOP 4.0.
sources.found: In 13 healthy adults over 536 nights, Oura Gen 3 and Gen 4 night-time resting heart rate (CCC 0.97-0.98) and HRV (CCC 0.97-0.99) agreed closely with ECG. WHOOP agreed moderately (CCC 0.91 for heart rate, 0.94 for HRV), while Polar (heart rate CCC 0.86, HRV 0.82) and Garmin HRV (0.87) agreed poorly.
sources.limitations: It has only 13 participants and one model per brand, results shifted with the analysis method, Oura promotes it and WHOOP disputes its methods; it was not counted because its direction was rated mixed.
sources.quote: Thirteen healthy adults (6 females) wore an ECG reference and multiple wearables simultaneously during sleep, totaling 536 nights.

verification.notes: No PMID was given. DOI 10.14814/phy2.70527 resolves to the Wiley Physiological Reports page 'Validation of nocturnal resting heart rate and heart rate variability in consumer wearables - Dial - 2025'. PMC12367097 has the same title, first author (Dial), journal and year (published 2025-08-20; 13(16):e70527). One secondary summary listed issue 13(23), probably confusing it with the follow-up letters. I could not find a PubMed record or PMID for the paper itself, so no PMID is supplied. Only first author Dial was seen; the rest of the author list (Hollander, Vatne, Emerson, Edwards, Hagen) was not confirmed. Two of the proposer's 'seen at' PubMed links point to other papers, not this one: PMID 41388834 / PMC12701519 is a letter by Grosicki and Presby (WHOOP, Inc.), 'Accurate comparison of wearables requires contextual equivalence', and PMID 41399178 is the authors' reply, 'Contextual equivalence for accurate comparison of wearables requires transparency' (DOI 10.14814/phy2.70706). These are commentary, not corrections. No erratum, correction or retraction was found. | The researcher's numbers match. The researcher's quote (design sentence: 'Thirteen healthy adults (6 females) wore an ECG reference and multiple wearables simultaneously during sleep, totaling 536 nights.') appeared word for word in search output, but it describes the design, not a result. Problems with the proposed statement: (1) the paper calls WHOOP's agreement 'moderate' for both RHR and HRV, so 'Oura and WHOOP agreed well' overstates WHOOP for this study; (2) Polar's HRV agreement was also poor (CCC 0.82), not just its RHR, which the statement omits. One search summary also reported alternative CCCs for HRV (Oura Gen 4 0.91, Gen 3 0.84, WHOOP 0.76), possibly from another analysis or table. A supplementary z-score table reportedly ranks Polar (0.92) above WHOOP (0.88) for RHR. Results depend on the analysis method. A WHOOP-authored letter (Grosicki & Presby) disputes the comparison methods, and the authors replied (PMIDs 41388834, 41399178, PMC12701519, PMC12706116). Those letters are not the paper. One search summary gave the paper's PMID as 40834291, but I did not see this on a PubMed page. Small n=13. Single Garmin model (Fenix 6), which the authors say should not be generalised to other Garmins.

sources.title: The Accuracy of Acquiring Heart Rate Variability from Portable Devices: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Dobbs WC, Fedewa MV, MacDonald HV, Holmes CJ, Cicone ZS, Plews DJ, Esco MR
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA) of portable-device HRV compared with ECG; literature searched up to 29 July 2017. 23 studies, 301 effects.
sources.population: Studies comparing portable HRV devices (chest straps, smartphone apps, wrist devices, etc.) with ECG in humans.
sources.sampleSize: 23 studies; 301 effect sizes (total participants not captured)
sources.found: Pooling 23 studies, HRV from portable devices differed from ECG by a small but significant amount (effect size 0.23, 95% CI 0.05-0.42), with large variation between studies (I² 78.6%). The size of the error depended on the HRV metric, body position and sex, but not on device type, and the authors judged it acceptable for field use.
sources.limitations: The literature runs only to 2017 and is mostly chest straps and apps rather than modern wrist or ring wearables during sleep, and the higher error for SDNN did not survive sensitivity analysis.
sources.quote: The aim was to quantify the accuracy of portable devices compared to electrocardiography (ECG) for measuring a multitude of HRV metrics and to identify potential moderators of this effect.

verification.notes: The PubMed record for PMID 30706234 is this paper: Dobbs WC et al., Sports Med 2019;49(3):417-435, DOI 10.1007/s40279-019-01061-5. The Altmetric record shows the same title, DOI, journal and first author (Ward C. Dobbs), dated January 2019, which is the online date; the print issue is March 2019. No PMCID was seen. A targeted search for retraction or erratum found none, and the PubMed record showed no notice. | Confirmed: PMID 30706234, Sports Med 2019;49(3):417-435, DOI 10.1007/s40279-019-01061-5, and the author list. The researcher's quote (the aims sentence) appeared word for word. The finding is stated accurately. Caveats: the included devices are mostly chest straps, apps and other portable devices, not specifically night-time consumer wrist or ring PPG. The SDNN effect on metric did not survive the sensitivity analysis, so the 'differs by metric' point is weaker for SDNN than for body position. The authors also conclude that the error is acceptable, which supports 'reasonable agreement' more than 'not interchangeable'. The literature runs only to 2017.

sources.title: Accuracy of Photoplethysmography-Derived Pulse Rate Variability Compared with Electrocardiography-Derived Heart Rate Variability: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Xu S, et al.
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of PPG-derived pulse rate variability compared with ECG-derived HRV (RMSSD, SDNN) in healthy or apparently healthy non-clinical populations. 43 studies in the qualitative synthesis (33 narrative); 10 unique studies pooled quantitatively (8 each for the RMSSD and SDNN meta-analyses).
sources.population: Healthy or apparently healthy non-clinical populations, mainly under resting or controlled conditions.
sources.sampleSize: 43 studies in the qualitative synthesis; 10 unique studies pooled (8 each for the RMSSD and SDNN meta-analyses); total participants not captured
sources.found: Pooling 10 studies of healthy people at rest, pulse rate variability from optical (PPG) sensors differed from ECG HRV by a small standardised error: 0.19 for RMSSD and 0.13 for SDNN. The authors warn against reading this as showing that PPG and ECG are interchangeable, or applying it to sleep, exercise or daily life.
sources.limitations: Few studies were pooled, all under resting or controlled conditions, so it says little directly about night-time wearable readings; it is also very recent and has not had a dedicated retraction check.
sources.quote: The pooled absolute standardized error was 0.188 (95% CI: 0.066 to 0.309; I^2 = 11.69%) for RMSSD and 0.134 (95% CI: 0.014 to 0.255; I^2 = 0%) for SDNN.

verification.notes: The PubMed record for PMID 42655500 is this paper: Sensors (Basel) 2026 Aug 17;26(16):5192, PMCID PMC13517957. The proposer gave no DOI; the DOI 10.3390/s26165192 was seen on doi.org with the same title. A search that did not name the author gave the first author as Shiwen Xu (PubMed). The full author list was not seen. The review is registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261426165). The pooled RMSSD and SDNN numbers and the warning against generalising them were confirmed in search snippets. The paper is very recent (Aug 2026). The PubMed and PMC records showed no notices, but no dedicated retraction search was run because the search budget was spent. | Confirmed: PMID 42655500, PMC13517957, Sensors 2026;26(16):5192, DOI 10.3390/s26165192 (the researcher left the DOI blank), first author Shiwen Xu. The researcher's quote matches word for word (only 'I^2' versus 'I2' formatting differs). One caveat on the researcher's wording: 'differed by metric' is not shown by the abstract. The RMSSD and SDNN CIs overlap almost completely, and I saw no formal test between metrics. The direction is also opposite to Dobbs 2019 (SDNN error larger there; RMSSD larger here). So the statement's 'error differs by HRV metric' is weakly supported. This source does support 'not equivalent/not interchangeable' and the explicit warning against generalising to sleep.

sources.title: Pulse rate variability is not the same as heart rate variability: findings from a large, diverse clinical population study
sources.authors: Kantrowitz, Ben-David, et al.
sources.design: Cross-sectional beat-to-beat agreement study comparing PPG pulse rate variability with ECG-derived HRV (criterion) using two Warfighter Monitor devices (chest and bicep). Time-domain indices SDNN, rMSSD and pNN50; Pearson correlation, Bland-Altman, and one-way ANOVA across chronic diseases. n=931 adults from a tertiary academic medical center in the southeastern US.
sources.population: Adults recruited from a tertiary academic medical center in the southeastern United States (diverse clinical population).
sources.found: In 931 adults at a hospital, optical pulse rate variability disagreed significantly with ECG HRV (p<0.001 for all comparisons), and the size of the gap varied across chronic diseases.
sources.limitations: It studied clinical patients using research-grade chest and arm sensors, not healthy people wearing consumer devices at night, so it did not count towards this claim.
sources.quote: Significant disagreement and differences were observed between ECG-HRV and PPG-PRV (p < 0.001 for all).

verification.notes: No PMID was given. DOI 10.3389/fphys.2025.1630032 resolves to the Frontiers in Physiology original research article (vol 16, article 1630032, published 30 July 2025). PMC12343505, USUHS and Univ. of Miami pages agree on title, first author (Kantrowitz, with Ben-David and Wittels among the authors), journal and year. I found no PubMed record or PMID for it; author initials were not seen. Caution: PubMed 42286401 is a different paper with a similar title, 'Pulse Rate Variability Is Not the Same as Heart Rate Variability: Implications for Sports Performance and Injury Prevention' (Sports Med Open 2026, DOI 10.1186/s40798-026-01027-8, 103 football athletes). Do not mix the two. A targeted search found no correction, erratum or retraction; the one retraction it returned was for an unrelated Frontiers article. | Confirmed: Front Physiol vol 16, published 2025-07-30, DOI 10.3389/fphys.2025.1630032, PMC12343505, first author Allen B. Kantrowitz. The researcher's summary of the finding is accurate. The researcher's quote is a background/introduction sentence, not a result, and I could not confirm it word for word: a targeted search for it did not return it, though one summary echoed the phrase 'PRV derived from PPG is not equivalent to HRV-derived from ECG'. Direction: the researcher's 'contradicts' is wrong relative to the PROPOSED statement. The paper supports its 'PRV is not equivalent to ECG HRV' clause and its caveat that clinical populations agree worse. findingSupported is fail only because the population (clinical, tertiary-care patients with chronic disease) and devices (research-grade Warfighter Monitor, not consumer wrist/ring wearables, not night-time) differ from the target population. Cite it as context for the clinical-population caveat, not as primary evidence for healthy adults. No PMID seen.

sources.title: Assessing the Accuracy of Popular Commercial Technologies That Measure Resting Heart Rate and Heart Rate Variability
sources.authors: Stone JD, ..., Hagen JA, et al.
sources.journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
sources.design: Validation study of seven commercial off-the-shelf devices/apps against a multi-lead ECG reference for resting-state HR and rMSSD (MAPE, Lin's CCC). n=5 healthy young adults, 148 total trials.
sources.population: Healthy young adults; devices included Oura, HRV4Training, CameraHRV and others.
sources.found: In 5 healthy young adults (148 trials), most of seven commercial devices and apps measured resting heart rate accurately. RMSSD accuracy varied widely: about 4-7% error for the best (HRV4Training, Oura) versus 112% for a smartphone camera app.
sources.limitations: With only five participants and daytime resting measurements, it cannot show how devices perform overnight or across a wider population.
sources.quote: Five healthy young adults generated 148 total trials.

verification.notes: No PMID was given, and none was found in PubMed or Europe PMC searches. DOI 10.3389/fspor.2021.585870 resolves to the Frontiers article ('ORIGINAL RESEARCH published: 01 March 2021'). PMC7956986, Frontiers and DOAJ agree on title, first author (Jason D. Stone), journal and year; the full author list was not captured. Accuracy note on the proposer's finding: the snippets say CameraHRV had the highest HR error (MAPE 17.26%) and 'the next highest was HRV4Training at 2.34%'. So 2.34% is the second-highest HR error, not the lowest, and 'MAPE from 2.34% (HRV4Training) to 17.26%' misstates the range. HRV4Training/ECG and Oura were the most accurate for rMSSD (under 7% error, CCC above 0.90), and CameraHRV's rMSSD MAPE was 112.36% with CCC 0.04. A targeted search found no retraction, erratum or correction. | Confirmed: Front Sports Act Living 2021;3:585870, DOI 10.3389/fspor.2021.585870, PMC7956986, first author Stone. Two searches described HRV4Training's 2.34% HR MAPE as the second-HIGHEST error after CameraHRV. The researcher's 'MAPE from 2.34% (HRV4Training) to 17.26%' therefore treats 2.34% as the lowest, which looks wrong; the rMSSD figures are correct. The researcher's quote ('An unfortunate consequence of their rapid commercialization...') was not seen in any search result. The design passes the criterion-validation definition, but n=5 is extremely small. Measurements were resting-state, not specifically nocturnal. No PMID seen. The paper supports 'accuracy depends on device' and acceptable Oura rMSSD agreement.

sources.title: Performance of seven consumer sleep-tracking devices compared with polysomnography
sources.authors: Chinoy ED, Cuellar JA, Huwa KE, Jameson JT, Watson CH, Bessman SC, et al.
sources.design: Laboratory validation study of seven consumer sleep trackers against polysomnography, with research actigraphy (Actiwatch) as a comparator, including nights with disrupted sleep. Sample size and number of nights not seen in the snippets.
sources.population: Healthy young adults. Devices: Fatigue Science Readiband, Fitbit Alta HR, Garmin Fenix 5S, Garmin Vivosmart 3, EarlySense Live, ResMed S+, SleepScore Max.
sources.found: In a laboratory comparison of seven consumer sleep trackers against polysomnography, the devices detected sleep very well (sensitivity at least 0.93) but wake poorly (specificity 0.18-0.54, lowest for the two Garmin models). Performance was worse on nights with disrupted sleep.
sources.limitations: It used a small laboratory sample of healthy adults, and its sleep-stage findings and exact sample size were not verified.
sources.quote: Sensitivity for devices versus PSG was very high (all ≥0.93)

verification.notes: DOI 10.1093/sleep/zsaa291 resolves to the OUP Sleep article with the same title (Sleep 2021;44(5):zsaa291). PMID 33378539 is tied to this paper (and DOI) by PubMed's reference linking on PMID 34340251 (Svetnik et al.), but the PubMed record page for 33378539 itself never appeared in results. The OUP, Monash, ResearchGate and citing-paper reference lists agree on title, first author Chinoy, journal and year. No PMCID was seen. The proposer's 'seen at' PubMed links are not this paper: 34340251 is a suvorexant/Alzheimer's wearable pilot that cites it, and 33782687 is the accompanying commentary 'Sleep-tracking technology in scientific research: looking to the future' (zsab071). Design details were confirmed in secondary sources: 34 adults (22 women, 28.1 ± 3.9 y), 3 nights, sensitivity ≥0.93, specificity 0.18-0.54. A targeted search found no retraction, erratum, correction or expression of concern. | Confirmed: Chinoy ED, Cuellar JA, Huwa KE, Jameson JT, Watson CH, Bessman SC, et al., Sleep 2021;44(5):zsaa291, DOI 10.1093/sleep/zsaa291. The PubMed search did not return the record, so PMID 33378539 is NOT confirmed. The researcher's 'seen at' PubMed links 34340251 and 33782687 are other papers (33782687 is 'Sleep-tracking technology in scientific research: looking to the future'). Not verified: n=34, 3 consecutive nights, the details of the sleep-stage comparisons, and 'most devices matched or beat actigraphy'. The verified quote is a phrase from search output, not a confirmed full sentence. The numbers in the proposed statement (sensitivity >=0.93, specificity 0.18-0.54) are supported.

sources.title: Performance of consumer wrist-worn sleep tracking devices compared to polysomnography: a meta-analysis
sources.authors: Lee YJ, Lee JY, Cho JH, Kang YJ, Choi JH
sources.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of consumer wrist-worn sleep trackers against polysomnography; databases searched to March 2024. 24 studies, 798 participants (devices included Fitbit, Jawbone, WHOOP, Garmin, Apple Watch, Xiaomi Mi Band 5).
sources.population: Participants in validation studies of Fitbit, Jawbone, WHOOP, Garmin, Apple Watch, Xiaomi Mi Band 5 and other wrist devices.
sources.found: Pooling 24 studies (798 participants), wrist-worn trackers' total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep latency and wake after sleep onset all differed significantly from polysomnography; for example, total sleep time differed by about 17 minutes and wake after sleep onset by about 13 minutes. The authors judge the devices useful for general sleep patterns but not as reliable as polysomnography.
sources.limitations: It covers wrist devices only (no rings), may include the same studies as Miller and Chinoy, and the direction of some errors was unclear.

verification.notes: The PubMed record for PMID 39484805 is this paper: Lee YJ et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2025 Mar 1;21(3):573-582, DOI 10.5664/jcsm.11460, PMCID PMC11874098 (embargoed until 2026-03-01). The JCSM DOI page and themednet agree. Authors seen: Lee YJ, Lee JY, Cho JH, Kang YJ, Choi JH. A targeted search found no retraction, erratum or correction. The pooled mean-difference numbers in the proposer's finding were not checked against the abstract in these results. | Confirmed: PMID 39484805, PMC11874098, J Clin Sleep Med 2025;21(3):573-582, DOI 10.5664/jcsm.11460. The researcher's numbers match. Not verified: Begg's/Egger's no publication bias for TST and sleep efficiency. Two search summaries disagreed on the direction of the WASO error (one said devices underestimated WASO, the other that WASO was higher on devices). The positive pooled mean difference fits the second, but the sign convention was not seen. The statement's claim only that the metrics 'differ significantly' is supported. No sentence was confirmed word for word, so verifiedQuote is null.

sources.title: Accuracy of Fitbit Charge 4, Garmin Vivosmart 4, and WHOOP Versus Polysomnography: Systematic Review
sources.authors: Schyvens et al.
sources.design: Systematic review (no meta-analysis seen) of validation studies of Fitbit Charge 4, Garmin Vivosmart 4 and WHOOP against PSG (or an ambulatory EEG monitor such as Sleep Profiler). 504 records screened; 8 articles included.
sources.population: Participants in PSG validation studies of Fitbit Charge 4, Garmin Vivosmart 4 and WHOOP.
sources.sampleSize: Number of studies and participants not captured
sources.found: A review of 8 validation studies found Fitbit Charge 4 and Garmin Vivosmart 4 moderately accurate against polysomnography. WHOOP was closest for total sleep time but furthest for REM sleep, and every device needed better sleep-stage classification.
sources.limitations: Only eight studies covering three devices were included, some used a home EEG headband instead of full polysomnography, and the review gives no pooled numbers.
sources.quote: the devices with higher relative agreement and sensitivities for multi-state sleep, Fitbit Charge 4 and WHOOP, seem appropriate to derive suitable estimates of sleep parameters

verification.notes: No PMID or DOI was given. PMC11004611 is this paper. The DOI 10.2196/52192 was seen for the JMIR mHealth and uHealth article e52192, published 2024-03-27; DOAJ and the Univ. A targeted search found no retraction, erratum or correction. | Confirmed: JMIR mHealth uHealth 2024;12:e52192, DOI 10.2196/52192 (researcher had none), PMC11004611, first author An-Marie Schyvens, published 2024-03-27. sources.title: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults
sources.authors: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, et al.
sources.citation: Br J Sports Med. 2018 Mar;52(6):376-384. Correction: Br J Sports Med. 2020;54(19):e7 (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608corr1; PMID 32943392; PMC7513243)
sources.design: Systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of RCTs (resistance exercise training of at least 6 weeks with dietary protein supplementation), 49 studies, 1,863 participants, with a two-phase breakpoint analysis of total protein intake vs change in fat-free mass. Br J Sports Med 2018; a 2020 correction is indexed (PMID 32943392, PMC7513243).
sources.population: Healthy adults doing resistance exercise training for at least 6 weeks, with dietary protein supplementation vs control; trained and untrained, young and older
sources.sampleSize: 49 RCTs, 1,863 participants. Per a secondary summary (Stronger by Science), the breakpoint analysis used about 42 study arms and 723 subjects.
sources.found: Pooling 49 randomised trials (1,863 people), adding protein during at least 6 weeks of resistance training increased fat-free mass gains by about 0.3 kg on average (95% CI 0.09 to 0.52). Gains levelled off at a total intake of about 1.6 g/kg/day; the effect was smaller in older people and larger in trained people (about 0.75 kg).
sources.limitations: The 1.6 g/kg/day figure comes from one breakpoint analysis that pooled trained and untrained, younger and older adults, so it is an imprecise average for the group and not a personal threshold.
sources.quote: With protein supplementation, protein intakes at amounts greater than ~1.6 g/kg/day do not further contribute RET-induced gains in FFM.

verification.notes: The PubMed search for PMID 28698222 returned this paper: Morton RW ... Phillips SM, Br J Sports Med 2018;52(6):376-384, DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608, PMCID PMC5867436. The PubMed record links an erratum. The correction appears on PubMed as PMID 32943392 and in PMC as PMC7513243 (Br J Sports Med 2020;54(19):e7, doi ...097608corr1). I could not see what the correction changed. Searches found no retraction and no expression of concern. The abstract's figures of 49 studies and 1,863 participants match the claim. I did not verify the breakpoint CI or the Stronger by Science figures. | PubMed record confirms the title, journal, year, design (RCTs only, RET of 6 weeks or more, two-phase breakpoint analysis) and 49 studies / 1,863 participants. I saw the 0.30 kg FFM effect, the 0.75 kg trained-subgroup effect (p=0.03) and the conclusion sentence quoted above in abstract snippets. I did not see the researcher's exact 1.62 g/kg/day sentence printed. A search on that exact phrase did return the BJSM abstract and PMC pages, which suggests the sentence exists, but I was not shown it, so quoteVerbatim is false. The 95% CI of roughly 1.0 to 2.2 g/kg/day comes from a later review by the same group (PMC5852756), not from the Morton abstract. The p=0.079 for the breakpoint comes from Stronger by Science (secondary). I did not see the 1RM, fibre CSA or mid-femur CSA numbers. I did not see what the 2020 correction changed. The pooled population mixes trained and untrained, young and older adults, so the 0.3 kg is an all-population estimate.

sources.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise
sources.authors: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, et al.
sources.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
sources.design: Position stand of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (an objective and critical review of protein intake for healthy, exercising individuals), published in the peer-reviewed Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, 2017;14:20.
sources.population: Exercising individuals, including resistance-trained people
sources.sampleSize: Not applicable (position stand drawing on the literature)
sources.found: This expert position stand concludes that a total intake of 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day is enough for most people who exercise to build and maintain muscle. It suggests that trained people who are cutting calories may need 2.3 to 3.1 g/kg/day to keep lean mass.
sources.limitations: It is an expert review, not new trial data, and it does not name a single best intake or a point beyond which more protein adds no muscle.
sources.quote: Higher protein intakes (2.3–3.1 g/kg/d) may be needed to maximize the retention of lean body mass in resistance-trained subjects during hypocaloric periods.

verification.notes: PMID 28642676 resolves on PubMed to this ISSN Position Stand (J Int Soc Sports Nutr, June 2017, DOI 10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8). The BMC/JISSN publisher page agrees on title, Jäger and Kerksick as first authors, vol 14, article 20, and 20 June 2017. The PMC page PMC5477153 also turned up. A targeted search for a retraction, erratum, correction or expression of concern found none for this paper. The only correction that surfaced belongs to the separate ISSN nutrient-timing position stand. The '1.4-2.0 g/kg/d' recommendation appeared in snippets. This is a position stand published in a peer-reviewed, PubMed-indexed journal. | The 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day sentence appeared only truncated in the PubMed snippet ('an overall daily protein intake in the range of 1.4-2.0 g protein/kg body weight/day (g/kg/d) is suffici...'). I never saw its opening clause ('For building muscle mass and for maintaining muscle mass through a positive muscle protein balance'), so the researcher's quote is not confirmed word for word. I did see the 2.3 to 3.1 g/kg/d hypocaloric sentence verbatim. I did not see the per-meal guidance (0.25 g/kg, 20 to 40 g, every 3 to 4 hours). The stand supports 1.6 g/kg/day as an adequate target, but its upper bound is 2.0, not 2.2, and it does not name 1.6 as a breakpoint. It also says (per news coverage of its points) that novel evidence suggests intakes above 3.0 g/kg/day may beneficially affect body composition in resistance-trained subjects, mainly through fat loss. That is a mild tension with the statement that intakes above 2.2 add no lean mass, so the wording should stay about lean mass specifically.

sources.title: Effects of 16 weeks of two different high-protein diets with either resistance or concurrent training on body composition, muscular strength and performance, and markers of liver and kidney function in resistance-trained males
sources.authors: Bagheri et al.
sources.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
sources.citation: J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2023 Dec;20(1):2236053
sources.design: Four-arm parallel 2x2 trial (resistance vs concurrent training x 1.6 vs 3.2 g/kg/day protein), 16 weeks, four sessions per week, n=48 resistance-trained males (age 26 ± 6 yr, BMI 25.6 ± 2.9), n=12 per arm. I did not see the word 'randomised' in the text I saw.
sources.population: Resistance-trained young men (age 26 ± 6 years, BMI 25.6 ± 2.9)
sources.found: In 48 resistance-trained young men over 16 weeks, 3.2 g/kg/day gave no more lean mass or strength than 1.6 g/kg/day. The one exception was a larger gain in peak power in one of the resistance-training groups. Kidney and liver markers did not change.
sources.limitations: With only 12 men per group, and randomisation not confirmed, it is too small to rule out modest differences, and it applies only to trained young men.

verification.notes: PMID 37516903 resolves on PubMed to this 16-week trial in resistance-trained males (J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2023, PMCID PMC10388821, DOI 10.1080/15502783.2023.2236053). The Taylor & Francis full-text page and PMC agree on title, journal, year and article number 2236053. Snippets confirmed n=48 (12 per group), age 26 ± 6 yr, BMI 25.6 ± 2.9, the 1.6 vs 3.2 g/kg/d arms and the 'appears sufficient to maximize' conclusion. I did not see the first author's initials or the full author list. No retraction, expression of concern or erratum surfaced on the PubMed or publisher results, but I ran no dedicated retraction search for this paper. | The design sentence I saw verbatim is: 'Forty-eight resistance-trained males (age: 26 ± 6 yr, body mass index: 25.6 ± 2.9 kg.m−2) performed 16 weeks (four sessions·w−1) of CT or RT with either 1.6 g.kg−1.d−1 protein (CT1; n = 12; RT1; n = 12) or 3.2 g.kg−1.d−1 protein (CT2; n = 12; RT2; n = 12).' The abstract text I saw did not say participants were randomised, so designStrong is unknown. Check the PMC methods before treating this as an RCT. The search summaries said the abstract contains the researcher's conclusion sentence, but they gave it only paraphrased, so quoteVerbatim is false. This is one small trial (12 per arm) in young trained men. It is underpowered to detect small lean-mass differences between 1.6 and 3.2 g/kg/day, so 'no additional benefit' is weak evidence of absence. A companion paper on the same cohort (PMC11349518) found that lean-mass changes were not associated with strength, endurance or power changes.

sources.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults
sources.authors: Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, et al.
sources.journal: Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle
sources.design: Systematic review with three-level random-effects meta-analyses and meta-regressions of 74 RCTs in healthy, non-obese adults who increased daily protein intake (PROSPERO CRD42020159001); J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2022;13(2):795-810.
sources.population: Healthy, non-obese adults who increased daily protein intake, most alongside resistance exercise; subgroups by age (<65 vs ≥65) and daily protein level
sources.found: Pooling 74 randomised trials in healthy adults, eating more protein alongside resistance exercise gave small extra lean-mass gains (standardised mean difference 0.22, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.30). The gains were more noticeable in younger people eating 1.6 g/kg/day or more. Effects on strength and physical function were small or unclear.
sources.limitations: It does not test whether gains stop above 1.6 g/kg/day, its results by age group were not verified, and a 2025 published letter questions its methods.
sources.quote: SMD = 0.22, 95% CI 0.14:0.30, n = 62 studies with RE, moderate certainty of the evidence

verification.notes: PMID 35187864 resolves on PubMed to this paper: Nunes EA ... Phillips SM, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2022 Apr;13(2):795-810, epub 20 Feb 2022, DOI 10.1002/jcsm.12922, PMCID PMC8978023. The Wiley page agrees. A search for a retraction or correction found none. Post-publication letters exist: a comment by Inca-Barriga, Alberti-Nuñez and López-Moreno (PMC12677926), and the authors' reply (PMID 41126611, DOI 10.1002/jcsm.70108, 2025). These are letters, not corrections. The quoted CI '0.09:0.35' does not contain the SMD of 0.40. That may be a typo in the paper or a transcription error, and I did not verify it. I did not verify the subgroup figures or the reply's SMDs. | Verified: 74 RCTs, three-level model, healthy non-obese adults, SMD 0.22 for LBM with resistance exercise, an effect more prominent in younger people at 1.6 g/kg/day or more, and the conclusion of 'small additional gains in LBM and lower body muscle strength'. The verifiedQuote is a fragment of an abstract sentence seen word for word, not a full sentence. NOT verified: the under-65 vs 65-and-over split, the claim of benefit at 1.2 to 1.59 g/kg/day in people 65 and over, the null result below 1.2 g/kg/day (4 trials), and the 2025 reply's SMDs (0.19 and 0.30). The proposed population text relies on the 65-and-over point, so findingSupported is unknown, not pass. The researcher's quote was given only paraphrased. Note that its reported CI (0.09 to 0.35) does not contain the point estimate of 0.40, which looks like a reporting error in the paper. Do not reproduce that CI in the app. Effects are SMDs, not kg. The paper supports a small effect and 1.6 g/kg/day as an adequate target in younger adults, but it does not test a plateau above 1.6. It has drawn a published 2025 methods critique (Inca-Barriga et al., on change-from-baseline effect sizes and multi-arm handling), and the authors replied.

sources.title: Dose-response relationship between protein intake and muscle mass increase: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
sources.authors: Tagawa R, Watanabe D, et al.
sources.design: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of RCTs using a multivariate spline model; Nutrition Reviews 2021;79(1):66-75 (Tagawa R, Watanabe D, Ito K, Ueda K, Nakayama K, Sanbongi C, Miyachi M). Includes trials with and without resistance training.
sources.population: Adults in RCTs of at least 2 weeks with differing protein doses, with and without resistance training
sources.sampleSize: 105 articles, 5,402 participants (counts reported by a later citing paper)
sources.found: Pooling randomised trials both with and without resistance training, each extra 0.1 g/kg/day of protein was linked to about 0.39 kg more lean mass below 1.3 g/kg/day, and about 0.12 kg above it. Gains slowed above 1.3 g/kg/day but did not stop, which points to diminishing returns up to about 3.5 g/kg/day rather than a ceiling at 1.6.
sources.limitations: It mixes people who did and did not do resistance training, so it cannot pinpoint the best intake for people training to build muscle.

verification.notes: The DOI 10.1093/nutrit/nuaa104 resolves on Oxford Academic to this title (Nutr Rev vol 79, issue 1, Jan 2021, pp 66-75), and PMC7727026 carries the same title. The direct PubMed search by PMID did not show the 33300582 record page. The PMID is corroborated indirectly: a Google Scholar lookup URL pairs doi nuaa104 with pmid 33300582, and a PubMed 'Cited by' listing shows PMID 33300582 as a 2020 Nutr Rev free PMC article. The online publication date was 2020, which is why some sources cite it as 2020. Semantic Scholar lists Tagawa and Watanabe as the first two authors; I did not see the rest of the author list. A medRxiv preprint of the same title exists (10.1101/2020.02.21.20026252); the cited version is the peer-reviewed journal article. One search snippet gave 5,411 subjects in 105 articles, against the claim's 5,402, so the participant count is unverified. The 0.39/0.12 kg per 0.1 g/kg/d spline result was confirmed in snippets. No retraction, expression of concern or erratum surfaced, but I ran no dedicated retraction search and did not view the PubMed record page. | The 0.39 and 0.12 kg per 0.1 g/kg/day figures and the 1.3 g/kg/day inflection appeared in search snippets of the abstract, but only paraphrased, so the researcher's quote is not confirmed word for word. I did not see the claim that the slowdown above 1.3 was 'markedly suppressed' by resistance training, or the 105-article / 5,402-participant counts. The PMID-targeted PubMed search returned no record for 33300582, so I used the PMC and OUP pages. I mark findingSupported as fail even though the numbers the researcher gives match what I saw, for three reasons. First, the population mixes trials with and without resistance training. Second, the outcome is a pooled association, not the resistance-trained breakpoint in the claim. Third, the continuing positive slope above 1.3 g/kg/day up to about 3.5 cuts against the proposed wording that 1.6 captures nearly all the gain and that intakes above 2.2 have not produced more lean mass. The paper supports diminishing returns, not a plateau, so the app text should acknowledge it rather than cite it as support for the ceiling.

sources.title: Synergistic Effect of Increased Total Protein Intake and Strength Training on Muscle Strength: A Dose-Response Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
sources.authors: Tagawa R, Watanabe D, Ito, Otsuyama, Nakayama, Sanbongi, Miyachi
sources.design: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of RCTs (random-effects model and spline model): 82 articles in the meta-analyses, 69 used for spline curves; Sports Medicine - Open 2022.
sources.population: Adults in RCTs of protein intake, with and without resistance training
sources.sampleSize: 82 articles in meta-analyses; 69 articles used for spline curves (participant total not seen)
sources.found: Extra protein increased strength only when combined with resistance training (about 2% more). With training, strength rose by about 0.72% per extra 0.1 g/kg/day up to 1.5 g/kg/day, with no further gain above that.
sources.limitations: It measures strength, not muscle mass, so it cannot confirm a muscle-mass target.
sources.quote: Muscle strength increase was significantly augmented only with resistance training (MD 2.01%, 95% CI 1.09-2.93) and was not augmented if resistance training was absent (MD 0.13%, 95% CI - 1.53 to 1.79).

verification.notes: PMID 36057893 resolves on PubMed to this paper by Ryoichi Tagawa, Daiki Watanabe et al. (Sports Med Open, published 4 Sep 2022, 8(1):110, DOI 10.1186/s40798-022-00508-w, PMCID PMC9441410). The Springer and PMC pages agree. The seven author surnames were seen: Tagawa, Watanabe, Ito, Otsuyama, Nakayama, Sanbongi, Miyachi. The 82 and 69 article counts, 0.72% per 0.1 g/kg/d up to 1.5 g/kg/d, and the 1.5 g/kg/d suggestion were confirmed in snippets. No retraction, expression of concern or erratum surfaced, but I ran no dedicated retraction search. | The researcher's numbers match what I saw. I mark findingSupported as fail because the outcome is muscle strength, not muscle mass or lean mass, which is what the claim is about. The researcher's quote ('Concurrent use of resistance training is essential...') did not appear in any result. It is useful context: strength also plateaus near 1.5 g/kg/day with resistance training, and protein adds nothing to strength without training. It should not be cited as evidence for the 1.6 g/kg/day lean-mass breakpoint. I did not see the participant total.

sources.title: Protein supplementation augments the adaptive response of skeletal muscle to resistance-type exercise training: a meta-analysis
sources.authors: Cermak NM, Res PT, de Groot LC, Saris WH, van Loon LJ
sources.design: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of protein supplementation during prolonged resistance-type exercise training in younger and older adults; AJCN 2012;96(6):1454-1464, DOI 10.3945/ajcn.112.037556 (Cermak NM, Res PT, de Groot LC, Saris WH, van Loon LJ). A news report gives 22 randomised controlled trials and 680 participants.
sources.population: Younger and older adults doing resistance-type exercise training for more than 6 weeks, with protein supplementation vs placebo
sources.sampleSize: 22 RCTs, 680 participants (per news report); an earlier abstract version reported 24 RCTs, 746 subjects
sources.found: This meta-analysis of protein supplements taken during prolonged resistance training reported an average extra fat-free mass gain of about 0.7 kg, plus greater leg-press strength. These figures come from press reports and a conference abstract and were not checked against the paper.
sources.limitations: It does not test how much total daily protein is needed, and its results could not be checked directly; they suggest the average extra gain may be larger than 0.3 kg, depending on which trials are included.

verification.notes: PMID 23134885 resolves on PubMed to this meta-analysis (Am J Clin Nutr 2012 Dec;96(6):1454-64). The PubMed result gave DOI 10.3945/ajcn.112.037556, which the source left out. Full author initials (Cermak NM, Res PT, de Groot LC, Saris WH, van Loon LJ) came from a ClinicalTrials.gov reference listing. The ACU research bank record agrees on title, journal, year and pages 1454-1464. No PMCID was seen. A targeted search for a retraction, erratum or expression of concern found none. I did not open the DOI on the AJCN publisher page itself. I did not verify the effect sizes (0.69 kg FFM, 13.5 kg leg press) or the participant counts from the news report. | The PubMed record confirms the citation, authors, DOI (the researcher left it blank) and the random-effects meta-analysis design. The snippets stopped before the results, so I could not verify the CI (0.47 to 0.91), the P value or the conclusion quote; findingSupported is unknown. It does not test a total-intake threshold, so 'context' is correct. Its pooled FFM effect (about 0.69 kg) is more than twice the 0.30 kg the proposed statement cites from Morton. If the app says the protein effect is 'around 0.3 kg', it should note that estimates range up to about 0.7 kg depending on the trials included.

sources.title: Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
sources.authors: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L
sources.design: A series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of prospective observational studies and clinical trials, with dose-response analyses. The counts (185 prospective studies, about 135 million person-years, 58 clinical trials, 4,635 adults) come from secondary news coverage shown in the search, not from abstract text I saw.
sources.population: Adults in prospective cohorts (general population) and adult participants in clinical trials
sources.sampleSize: 185 prospective studies (just under 135 million person-years) and 58 clinical trials (4,635 adult participants)
sources.found: A series of reviews of prospective studies and clinical trials found that people who ate the most fibre had 15 to 30% lower all-cause and cardiovascular death, and lower rates of coronary heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer, than people who ate the least. The biggest risk reductions were at about 25 to 29 g a day, and trials showed lower body weight, systolic blood pressure and total cholesterol with more fibre.
sources.limitations: The findings on disease and death are observational, so they cannot prove fibre is the cause; a published correction exists but its content was not checked, and the dose-response curves above about 30 g a day are uncertain.
sources.quote: Observational data suggest a 15–30% decrease in all-cause and cardiovascular related mortality, and incidence of coronary heart disease, stroke incidence and mortality, type 2 diabetes, and colorectal cancer when comparing the highest dietary fibre consumers with the lowest consumers.

verification.notes: The PubMed record for PMID 30638909 matches: Reynolds A, Mann J, Cummings J, Winter N, Mete E, Te Morenga L. Lancet 2019 Feb 2;393(10170):434-445, doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9, Epub 10 Jan 2019. The Dundee repository copy agrees on the volume, pages and DOI. PubMed has a linked 'Department of Error' notice (PMID 30712898), so an erratum exists. I did not see what the erratum corrects, and I did not confirm the page (406) or DOI (10.1016/S0140-6736(19)30119-9) that the citation gives for it. A search on the title with retraction, expression of concern and erratum terms found no retraction or expression of concern. No PMCID was seen. | PMID, authors, journal and pages match. A Department of Error notice (PMID 30712898) is linked to the record. I did not see its content, and no retraction appeared. An exact-phrase search for the researcher's 25-29 g sentence returned the PubMed abstract and the Lancet full text as top hits, and HealthDay carried near-identical wording, but the sentence was never displayed to me word for word, so quoteVerbatim is false. I saw the 15-30% sentence and the dose-response sentence in the search output. I could not verify the claim that secondary coverage rates the certainty of evidence as 'moderate'.

sources.title: Dietary fibre intake and risk of cardiovascular disease: systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Threapleton DE, Greenwood DC, Evans CEL, Cleghorn CL, Nykjaer C, Woodhead C, et al.
sources.design: Systematic review and random-effects dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies with at least 3 years of follow-up. 22 cohort study publications.
sources.population: Adults free of CVD at baseline in prospective cohorts (Europe, US, Japan, Australia)
sources.found: Across 22 cohort study publications, each extra 7 g of fibre a day was linked to about 9% lower risk of cardiovascular disease and of coronary heart disease (relative risk 0.91 for both). Insoluble fibre, cereal fibre and vegetable fibre were also linked to lower risk.
sources.limitations: These are observational data with moderate differences between studies, so other features of a high-fibre diet or lifestyle may explain part of the link.

The McMaster experts page confirms the journal, volume, pages and DOI. Searching for retraction, erratum, correction and expression of concern found none. sources.title: Current WHO recommendation to reduce free sugar intake from all sources to below 10% of daily energy intake for supporting overall health is not well supported by available evidence

sources.found: This review argues that the 10% limit is poorly supported for overall health. In its account, the evidence linking sugar to obesity comes mostly from sugary drinks, and studies of sugar in solid foods mostly found no effect.
sources.limitations: It is a narrative rather than a systematic review, a correction was later published, and other researchers said it misrepresented their work.

The missing fields come from the PubMed correction notice PMID 36200570, which names the original article (authors Rina Ruolin Yan, Chi Bun Chan, Jimmy Chun Yu Louie) as Am J Clin Nutr 2022 Jul 6;116(1):15-39, doi 10.1093/ajcn/nqac084, and links it to PMID 35380611. It therefore does not support the proposed statement, and findingSupported is fail. A letter by Hieronimus and Stanhope disputed how the review represented their work, and the authors did not reply. sources.title: Effect of longer term modest salt reduction on blood pressure: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
sources.authors: He FJ, Li J, MacGregor GA

sources.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of modest salt reduction lasting 4 or more weeks (BMJ 2013;346:f1325, PMID 23558162; also Cochrane CD004937.pub2). sources.found: In trials lasting at least four weeks, eating about 4.4 g less salt a day lowered systolic blood pressure by about 4.2 mm Hg and diastolic by about 2.1 mm Hg. The fall was larger in people with high blood pressure (about 5.4 mm Hg systolic) than in those with normal blood pressure (about 2.4 mm Hg).
sources.limitations: Results varied a lot between trials (I² 75%), and many of its trials are also in the other reviews, so it is not fully independent evidence.
sources.quote: A modest reduction in salt intake for 4 or more weeks causes significant and, from a population viewpoint, important falls in BP in both hypertensive and normotensive individuals

verification.notes: PMID 23558162 resolves to He FJ, Li J, MacGregor GA, 'Effect of longer term modest salt reduction on blood pressure: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials', BMJ 2013;346:f1325, DOI 10.1136/bmj.f1325. A search of the title with retraction, correction and erratum terms found no notice. Only letters and rapid responses were seen. Those results came from bibliographic pages, so the check is not exhaustive. | The numbers I saw match the researcher's on the urinary sodium fall, the 4.4 g salt equivalent, the pooled SBP and DBP, the hypertensive SBP with CI and I2, and the normotensive SBP and DBP. Some figures came from a PubMed-indexed commentary (PMID 24192084) and a Cochrane abstract snippet. I did not see the normotensive SBP CI (-3.56 to -1.29), I2=66% or the 3 g/day target. The fall was larger in older people, non-white people and people who started with higher blood pressure, and short trials underestimated the effect.
sources.limitations: It includes very short trials and shares many trials with He 2013, and its trial and participant totals were confirmed only from a paper that cites it.
sources.quote: Reductions in blood pressure were observed in diverse population subsets examined, including hypertensive and non-hypertensive individuals.

Title, authors, journal and year agree across PMC, the NHS medicines resources page, the George Institute page and the QMUL repository. I verified the 1.10 mm Hg per 50 mmol figure, the subgroup modifiers (older, non-white, higher baseline SBP) and the conclusion that short trials underestimate the effect. sources.title: Effect of lower sodium intake on health: systematic review and meta-analyses
sources.authors: Aburto NJ, Ziolkovska A, Hooper L, Elliott P, Cappuccio FP, Meerpohl JJ

sources.found: In adults, eating less sodium lowered systolic blood pressure by about 3.4 mm Hg and diastolic by about 1.5 mm Hg, and going below 2 g of sodium a day lowered systolic pressure by about 3.5 mm Hg. It found no significant harm to blood fats.
sources.limitations: The split between people with and without high blood pressure was not confirmed from this review, and its main figure was seen in a UK government report that cites it rather than in the abstract itself.
sources.quote: systolic blood pressure was reduced by 3.47 mm Hg (0.76 to 6.18) and diastolic blood pressure by 1.81 mm Hg (0.54 to 3.08)

The researcher's 3.39 mm Hg figure matches the SACN report's citation of Aburto 2013. sources.title: Effect of reduced dietary sodium on blood pressure: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
sources.authors: Midgley JP, Matthew AG, Greenwood CM, Logan AG

The JAMA abstract, reached through a library proxy, confirms the finding: a 100 mmol/d sodium reduction lowered blood pressure by 3.7/0.9 mm Hg in hypertensive trials and 1.0/0.1 mm Hg in normotensive trials, and publication bias was evident. The 56-trial basis is mentioned in a JAMA letter. sources.title: Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses
sources.authors: Lane MM, Gamage E, Du S, Ashtree DN, McGuinness AJ, Gauci S, Baker P, Lawrence M, Rebholz CM, Srour B, Touvier M, Jacka FN, O'Neil A, Segasby T, Marx W
sources.design: Umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses (mostly observational, largely prospective cohort data), with evidence-class grading (I-IV/V) plus GRADE; 45 unique pooled analyses (13 dose-response, 32 non-dose-response), n=9,888,373. BMJ 2024;384:e077310, PMID 38418082.
sources.population: Adults and children in observational studies worldwide; NOVA-defined UPF exposure; searches 2009 to June 2023 (MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, Cochrane)
sources.sampleSize: 14 meta-analyses, 45 unique pooled analyses (13 dose-response, 32 non-dose-response); n = 9,888,373
sources.found: This umbrella review pooled 45 analyses covering about 9.9 million people. Higher ultra-processed food intake was linked to higher risk of cardiovascular death (RR 1.50, very low certainty), type 2 diabetes (RR 1.12 in dose-response analysis, moderate certainty) and anxiety. Evidence was weaker for death from any cause (RR 1.21, low certainty), depression and obesity.
sources.limitations: It rests on observational studies with mostly self-reported diet and overlapping cohorts, so it shows association, not cause, and most outcomes were rated low or very low certainty.
sources.quote: cardiovascular disease related mortality (risk ratio 1.50, 95% confidence interval 1.37 to 1.63; GRADE=very low) and type 2 diabetes (dose-response risk ratio 1.12, 1.11 to 1.13; moderate)

verification.notes: The PubMed record for PMID 38418082 matches: Lane MM et al., 'Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses', BMJ 2024;384:e077310 (28 Feb 2024), DOI 10.1136/bmj-2023-077310, PMCID PMC10899807. The BMJ publisher page and the JCU and Bond repository pages agree. My search for a correction, retraction, erratum or expression of concern found none. A PubMed comment exists (PMID 38531598, 'other approaches and evidence needed to prove genuine causal effect'), but it is commentary, not a notice. One secondary site (lifespan.io) cites the article number wrongly as e077210; that is its own typo, not an erratum. | Identity confirmed (Lane MM et al., BMJ 2024, PMID 38418082, PMC10899807). Search snippets showed the key abstract numbers: CVD mortality RR 1.50 (very low), T2D dose-response RR 1.12 (moderate), all-cause mortality RR 1.21 (low), heart disease mortality HR 1.66 (low). These match the researcher's statement, including that T2D is the only moderate-GRADE outcome and that most outcomes are low or very low. Not seen: '14 meta-analyses' and '32 of 45 (71%)'. Quote: a search summary gave '45 unique analyses, including 13 dose-response associations and 32 nondose-response associations (n=9,888,373)'. That is close to the quote but not word for word, so quoteVerbatim is false. The verifiedQuote is a fragment of the class I sentence, not a full sentence. No retraction or erratum notice was seen, but the PubMed page was not displayed in full. Published critiques (e.g., Munafo, PMID 38531598) note that the evidence is associational.

sources.title: Ultra-processed foods and human health: An umbrella review and updated meta-analyses of observational evidence
sources.authors: Dai S, Wellens J, Yang N, Li D, Wang J, Wang L, et al.

sources.population: RCTs of interventions to modify UPF intake (3 educational interventions, 1 controlled feeding trial in weight-stable adults)
sources.found: This review found only 4 randomised trials, with 455 participants followed for a median of 12 weeks: 3 education programmes and 1 controlled feeding trial. There was no significant effect for 30 of 42 outcomes. Eating less ultra-processed food lowered energy intake and weight in the feeding trial, and weight and waist size in the education trials, at low to varying certainty.
sources.limitations: The trials are too few, small and short to confirm or rule out health effects, and the single feeding trial is probably Hall 2019, so it is not independent evidence.
